title: Preterm RDS: escalating support on CPAP
objective: Manage non-invasive support (CPAP, NIPPV, high-flow nasal cannula), conventional and high-frequency ventilation, and therapeutic gases, and prevent complications of respiratory support
secondaryObjectives: Recognize respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency -- tachypnea, grunting, flaring, retractions, cyanosis -- and expect it to worsen over the first days before improving
Explain how antenatal corticosteroids, exogenous surfactant, CPAP and caffeine change the course of RDS, and assist with surfactant given through the endotracheal tube
Support retinopathy of prematurity screening for at-risk infants and keep oxygen saturation within ordered targets, because excess oxygen contributes to ROP

brief.situation: Handover at 09:00 in the NICU. A boy born at 30 weeks, 1,400 g, now one hour old. His mother had one dose of antenatal steroids before a fast labor. He was started on CPAP 6 cmH2O in the delivery room. Admission temperature 36.7. Ordered oxygen saturation target 90-94%.
handover: On CPAP 6 by nasal prongs, FiO2 0.30, SpO2 92%, HR 158, RR 68.
Grunting, nasal flaring and subcostal retractions since birth. Chest X-ray: ground-glass lungs with air bronchograms.
The unit protocol lets the nurse set CPAP between 5 and 8 cmH2O and titrate FiO2 to the saturation target. Surfactant needs the neonatologist.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Change the oxygen and the CPAP pressure in small steps, then watch the saturation. The 15-minute checks are waits you can skip to.
Look at the baby and the equipment as well as the numbers.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. The case ends at the four-hour review, then a debrief scores what you did.

whatNow.question: What is happening to this baby's lungs, and what do you do next and why?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: Names respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency in a 30-week infant, worsening as expected in the first hours, citing grunting, flaring, retractions, a rising oxygen need and the X-ray; may note the incomplete antenatal steroids.
parts.modelAnswer: RDS from surfactant deficiency: 30 weeks with only one steroid dose, grunting, flaring and retractions, a ground-glass X-ray, and an oxygen need that keeps rising, as RDS does over the first hours.

parts.label: Next steps
parts.criteria: Keeps CPAP at 6-8 cmH2O (raising it within protocol), checks the interface, titrates FiO2 to SpO2 90-94% and avoids hyperoxia, and escalates for surfactant (LISA preferred) because FiO2 is above 0.30 on CPAP of at least 6; plans a blood gas.
parts.modelAnswer: Check the prongs and seal, raise CPAP toward 7-8, titrate oxygen to 90-94% and no higher, and call the neonatologist now: FiO2 above 0.30 on CPAP 6 or more is the threshold for surfactant, preferably by LISA so he stays on CPAP. Send a gas.

source.note: Neonatologist called within 15 min of the surfactant threshold.

noProgress.rationale: A preterm baby still needing about half oxygen at four hours with no surfactant is untreated RDS heading for ventilation, so this case calls it harm.

stableLate.narrative: He is settled at four hours, but the route cost something: late surfactant, a breathing tube, a long time above the saturation target, or slipped prongs left too long.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: named RDS and the surfactant threshold

expertPath.text: Assess: grunting, flaring, retractions; RDS. Check the prongs. Raise CPAP to 7 within protocol.
FiO2 creeps above 0.30 on CPAP 6 or more: call the neonatologist for surfactant by LISA. Send a gas.
Surfactant given by LISA. Over the next 30 minutes the oxygen need falls fast: wean FiO2 in small steps to keep 90-94%.
Saturation drops: look before turning up the oxygen. The prongs have slipped: reposition, chin strap, suction.
On CPAP in low oxygen at the review.

collapse.headline: Hypoxic collapse
collapse.body: Find when the saturation first fell and what was done: a slipped interface, a threshold missed, or oxygen not turned up while help was called.

stable.headline: Stable on CPAP after surfactant
stable.body: CPAP held at 6-8, surfactant by LISA at the threshold, the interface checked before more oxygen, and the oxygen weaned to 90-94% as the lungs opened. That is the expert path.

stableLate.headline: Stable, by a harder route
stableLate.body: He is settled, but check when surfactant came, whether he needed a tube, how long he sat above 95% on oxygen, and how long the prongs were out.

time_up.headline: Untreated RDS
time_up.body: The oxygen need kept rising. FiO2 above 0.30 on CPAP of at least 6 is the threshold to ask for surfactant.

scoring.modelReasoning: Respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency in a 30-week infant with incomplete antenatal steroids: grunting, flaring, retractions and a rising oxygen need in the first hours, with a ground-glass X-ray. Support with CPAP at about 6-8 cmH2O and titrate oxygen to a saturation of 90-94%, avoiding hyperoxia because excess oxygen contributes to retinopathy of prematurity. When FiO2 exceeds 0.30 on CPAP of at least 6, ask for surfactant; LISA is the preferred route for a spontaneously breathing baby on CPAP, at 200 mg/kg of poractant for rescue. After surfactant the oxygen need falls within minutes, so wean promptly. A sudden desaturation calls for a look at the baby and the interface before more oxygen.

afterSurf.ask: While surfactant is set up: what will his oxygen need do in the 30 minutes after the dose?

choices.label: Fall quickly: be ready to wean
Stay about the same for hours

afterSurf.explain: It falls quickly as the alveoli stay open. Wean FiO2 in small steps to keep 90-94%; leaving it high pushes saturations above 95% on extra oxygen, which contributes to retinopathy of prematurity.

target.ask: What saturation range are you titrating to for this 30-week baby in oxygen?
target.explain: 90-94%, with alarms at 89% and 95%. Higher saturations on extra oxygen add retinopathy risk; lower ones add mortality risk.

Intubate, give it, and ventilate for a day

lisa.explain: LISA: a thin catheter placed in the trachea while he breathes on CPAP, so he avoids mechanical ventilation.
